# 0108-xds-sds-validation-context

Phase 65. Proves that a **CertificateValidationContext delivered over SDS is the
ACTUAL downstream mTLS trust anchor** — not merely that both proxies agree.

The second SDS resource type (after phase 60.2's `tls_certificate` server cert,
fixture `0103`, whose topology this clones) and the third xDS-family row.

## Topology

```
                      SDS (SotW StreamSecrets, h2c)          in-memory,
  driver ──dial──▶ [ proxy: l_sds_mtls ] ◀── sds_cluster ──▶ driver-owned
   (2 arms)          tcp_proxy                                sdsserver.Server
                        │                                     (ONE per side)
                        ▼
                    c_backend (TCP echo)
```

One TLS-terminating `tcp_proxy` listener. Its `DownstreamTlsContext` carries:

- `require_client_certificate: true`
- a **STATIC** server cert (`tls_certificates`, `inline_string`), and
- `validation_context_sds_secret_config` naming secret `validation_ca`, fetched
  over a SotW SDS gRPC stream against `sds_cluster`.

Only the validation context arrives via SDS, so boot's SDS pre-scan sees exactly
one secret (`seen==1`) and the deferred compose-two edge is never touched
(PLAN-65 D3). Each side gets its **own** SDS receiver — a shared one would let
one side's fetch contaminate the other's view
(`reference_periodic_sink_differential_two_receivers`).

Reference: Envoy contrib-v1.37.2, `STRICT_DNS` via `host.docker.internal`,
listener port **10444**. Subject: envoy-go, `STATIC`, loopback.

## The PKI — in memory, per run; there is no `pki/` dir

Five artifacts, generated by `ensure()` with `crypto/x509` (ECDSA P-256, the
`0018` `pki/gen.go` crypto shape), **none of which touch disk**:

| artifact | issuer | role |
|---|---|---|
| `CA_served` | self | **the anchor under test** — served over SDS as `trusted_ca` |
| server leaf | `CA_served` | `ServerAuth`, SAN `DNS:l_sds_mtls.fixture.test`; injected `inline_string` into both yamls |
| `client_good` | `CA_served` | `ClientAuth` — **must be ACCEPTED** |
| `CA_unserved` | self | **never delivered to either proxy** |
| `client_bad` | `CA_unserved` | `ClientAuth` — **must be REJECTED** |

**Why no `pki/` dir** (PLAN-65 D2). Neither parent's model fits. `0103` commits
its PEMs (and has no client-cert precedent at all); `0018` generates at `init()`
and `.gitignore`s the output (needing file I/O and gitignore upkeep). `0108`
needs five artifacts including two client keys — committing them is the worst
option, and generating them on disk buys nothing, because nothing here needs a
file:

- the server cert is injected **`inline_string:`** into both bootstraps (no
  `HostMount`, no Docker mount);
- the CA goes out over SDS as `inline_bytes` — already in memory;
- the client certs feed the driver's own `tls.Config` — already in memory.

Per-run freshness is safe: the observable is an accept/reject verdict, not
`0103`'s `serial=`/`san=` identity.

> `inline_string`, **not** `inline_bytes`, in the YAML: `inline_bytes` is a proto
> `bytes` field and protojson demands base64, while `inline_string` takes PEM text
> directly. The multi-line PEM is injected under a block scalar (`inline_string: |`)
> via the driver's `indentPEM` helper — a raw `fmt.Sprintf` would leave every
> continuation line at column 0 and produce invalid YAML.
>
> Note also that the two PEM substitution keys are documented in the YAML headers
> **without** their template-action braces. `text/template` expands actions inside
> YAML comments too, and a multi-line PEM expanded into a `#` comment splatters its
> continuation lines out of the comment — this bit during Task 8 and cost a boot
> failure that looked like an indentation bug.

## The two arms (the observable)

Both arms fold into ONE byte stream (`CompareBytes` compares a single `[]byte`
per side). Both sides must emit, byte-identically:

```
good=ok echo=phase65-mtls-probe
bad=rejected
```

1. **positive** — dial presenting `client_good` (chains to the SERVED CA):
   handshake succeeds, write `phase65-mtls-probe\n`, read the echo back through
   `tcp_proxy`. The backend IS exercised here (unlike `0103`); `BackendCount()`
   returns 1 (`reference_differential_backendcount_min_one`).
2. **negative** — dial presenting `client_bad` (chains to the UN-SERVED CA): the
   round trip MUST fail → `bad=rejected`. If it unexpectedly succeeds the driver
   records `bad=ACCEPTED` — the exact accept-all signal this fixture exists to
   catch.

Each arm drives the **full round trip**, not just the handshake: under TLS 1.3
the server's verdict on the client cert arrives *after* the client's
`Handshake()` has already returned, so a handshake-only probe would mis-report a
rejection as success. The dial is inlined in the driver because neither
`helpers.TLSServedLeaf` nor `helpers.TLSRoundTrip` can present a client cert —
neither has a `Certificates` field nor a parameter to supply one.

## ⚠️ Why the driver carries a structural check

`CompareBytes` alone would make the proposition under test *"both sides agree"* —
which is **not** the same as *"the served CA is the anchor"*. The breaks that
matter are **symmetric**: changing the served CA, or re-signing `client_bad` with
it, changes **both sides identically**, so the two streams still compare EQUAL
and a pure-`CompareBytes` fixture passes green
(`reference_vacuous_break_receiver_normalizes`).

This was confirmed empirically, not assumed: with `structuralCheck` disabled, the
served-CA break **passes**. So `driveSide` asserts each side's OWN bytes against
the single correct stream and returns an error on any deviation; the runner turns
that into `t.Fatalf("<side> drive: ...")`, naming the side and the violated arm.
Both arms are checked independently and all violations are reported together
(`reference_fatalf_makes_assertions_unreachable`).

Because exactly one structurally-valid stream exists, the structural check
strictly **subsumes** `CompareBytes` here: any deviation trips it first.
`CompareBytes` is retained as the harness-standard cross-side leg and was proven
live by isolating it (asymmetric break with the structural check disabled → a
mismatch at byte offset 5).

## Why the failure text is normalized

The reference (BoringSSL) sends the TLS alert `unknown ca`; envoy-go (Go
`crypto/tls`) sends `bad certificate`. **A driver asserting the error string
cross-side fails 100% of the time** (PLAN-65 C3). The negative arm records only
the stable token `rejected` (the `0045` `closeOK` idiom).

The reject can also surface as `client didn't provide a certificate`: Go's TLS
client withholds a cert that does not match the `CertificateRequest`'s
acceptable-CA hint — a hint itself derived from the SDS-served CA. Same
proposition, different manifestation; normalizing is what makes the arm portable.

## Coverage boundary: no `ssl.*` stats

The SPEC designed the negative arm around a subject-side
`listener.….ssl.fail_verify_error >= 1` assertion. **That counter does not exist
in envoy-go** — it emits no `ssl.*` stats whatsoever (the only listener-scope
counter is `downstream_cx_total`), so the assertion cannot be written (PLAN-65
C3). This is a pre-existing framework gap that phase 65 neither opens nor closes;
it is recorded as a deferred Observability/xDS candidate.

The accept/reject contrast discharges the obligation and is strictly **stronger**
than the stat would have been: a subject-only counter proves nothing cross-side.

## Running

Always use the FULL selector (`reference_differential_run_selector` — a bare
`-run '0108'` matches ZERO subtests and reports a vacuous green):

```bash
go test ./test/differential/ -count=1 -run 'TestDifferential/0108-xds-sds-validation-context' -v
```
